passage:
Sunday: Playing ludo with his sister Nikita, five-year-old Gautam blew on the dice three times and whispered, "Six, six, six." He rolled a two. Next time he blew harder.
Wednesday: He made a new rule. He tapped the dice on his nose before every roll. When a six came, he shouted, "See? Nose magic!"
Saturday: Nikita rolled a six without touching her nose. Gautam frowned, then tapped his nose twice, just to be safe, and smiled when his turn came.

qa.q: What did Gautam tap the dice on before every roll?
qa.a: He tapped the dice on his nose.

qa.q: Why might Gautam keep tapping his nose even after Nikita rolled a six without it?
qa.a: Believing in nose magic makes the game feel in his hands, and that feels safer and more fun than plain luck. 😊

qa.q: How could Nikita or a parent gently help Gautam notice how dice work?
qa.a: They could play a round where everyone rolls with and without nose taps and count the sixes together, keeping it playful.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel about Gautam's nose magic?
qa.a: Nikita might find it funny, or a bit annoying when Gautam claims the credit for a lucky six.

grounding: A young boy believes blowing on or tapping the dice brings sixes, and keeps the ritual because it comforts him.

passage:
The cricket final on TV was in its last over when the power went out. Tanvir groaned and grabbed his phone to check the score, but the signal kept dropping.
Five-year-old Sudha ran to the kitchen and came back holding the steel spoon she always held during matches. She squeezed it with both hands and shut her eyes tight. "If I don't let go, we win," she said.
Tanvir finally got the score. "We won!"
Sudha opened her eyes and hugged the spoon. "I did it."
Tanvir laughed and let her keep the credit.

qa.q: What did Sudha hold during the match?
qa.a: The steel spoon she always held during matches.

qa.q: Why did Sudha squeeze the spoon with her eyes shut during the power cut?
qa.a: With the screen dark and nothing to watch, holding the spoon made her feel she could still help the team win.

qa.q: What could Tanvir say later to gently widen Sudha's idea?
qa.a: He could ask playfully whether children on the other side were holding spoons too, and say cheering is fun even though spoons don't decide scores.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir let Sudha keep the credit?
qa.a: He can see how happy and in charge the spoon makes her feel, and the win doesn't need correcting in that moment. 😊

grounding: A young girl squeezes a lucky spoon during a power cut, believing it made her team win.

passage:
On the terrace of their Chennai flat, Shankar watched the colony boys' cricket match below. His team, the Blue Stars, were losing. Shankar, five, pulled off his T-shirt, turned it inside out and put it back on.
"Why inside out?" asked his appa, Lokesh.
"So they win."
Two wickets fell. Shankar hopped on one foot. The Blue Stars hit a four, and he hopped faster. When they lost anyway, he looked down at his foot, puzzled.
Lokesh sat down beside him. "Want to hop for the next match too?"
"Yes. Harder," Shankar said.

qa.q: What did Shankar do to his T-shirt?
qa.a: He turned it inside out and put it back on.

qa.q: What does Shankar's plan to hop 'harder' next time suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he still believes his actions steer the match, and feeling in charge is more comforting than accepting he can't change it.

qa.q: How could Lokesh support Shankar without mocking the ritual?
qa.a: He could enjoy the hopping with him but also point to what the players did, like hitting the four, so Shankar sees who really plays the game.

qa.q: How might the Blue Stars players feel if they knew about Shankar's hopping?
qa.a: They would probably be touched to have such a keen fan, even though their own batting and bowling decided the match.

grounding: A small boy turns his shirt inside out and hops, believing it will make his colony team win.

passage:
"Wait, Indu didi! I have to do the magic first."
Vaibhav kissed the dice, spun around once and whispered, "Ladder, ladder, ladder."
"It's just a dice, Vaibhav."
"No! If I say it three times, it listens." He rolled a four, and his counter climbed the ladder. "See? It listened!"
"And last time? You said it and got the big snake."
"Last time I only spun half."
Papa laughed from the sofa. "And when Indu rolls without magic?"
Vaibhav thought hard. "That's her turn. It's different." He hugged the dice before passing it over.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav whisper before he rolled?
qa.a: He whispered, "Ladder, ladder, ladder."

qa.q: Why does Vaibhav hug the dice and insist on doing the magic first?
qa.a: Doing the magic makes Vaibhav feel in charge of the roll, which feels safe and exciting, so when a ladder comes he is sure his words made it happen 😊

qa.q: What choice could Papa make next to help Vaibhav notice how the dice really works, without spoiling the game?
qa.a: Papa could build on his own question: everyone counts ladders for a few rounds, with magic and without, so Vaibhav can see for himself that the dice does the same either way.

qa.q: How might Indu feel when Vaibhav says the dice listened to him?
qa.a: Indu may feel amused or a little annoyed, because she knows it is just a dice and remembers the big snake he got last time even with the magic.

grounding: It shows a young child believing that a whispered spell and a spin can make the dice give a ladder, and how comforting that feels.

passage:
Teacher's note, UKG sports practice (Ms Rao)
During tug-of-war today, Dhruv, 5, would not hold the rope. He stood behind the Green team with his eyes shut, fingers crossed on both hands, hopping on one foot. When I asked why, he said, "If I hop ten times, Green wins."
Green lost. Dhruv's face crumpled. "I counted wrong," he said. Manoj told him, "Hopping doesn't pull the rope." Dhruv shouted, "It does if you do it right!"
I asked the Green team to try once with every hand on the rope. They pulled together and won. Dhruv grinned but said the hops helped too. Tomorrow we will talk about what moved the rope.

qa.q: What did Dhruv say would happen if he hopped ten times?
qa.a: He said, "If I hop ten times, Green wins."

qa.q: How does Dhruv feel when Green loses, and why does he keep believing in the hopping?
qa.a: Dhruv feels upset, his face crumpling, but he blames his counting instead of the idea and shouts that hopping works if you do it right.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms Rao was a turning point, and why?
qa.a: Asking for every hand on the rope let Dhruv feel the team actually pull and win, a gentle way to show what changes the result without mocking the hops.

qa.q: What is it like for Manoj to be on the team while Dhruv hops at the back?
qa.a: Manoj may feel frustrated, because one fewer person is pulling and Manoj can plainly see that hopping does not move the rope.

grounding: It shows a young child believing a hopping ritual can decide a tug-of-war result, and holding on to it because it feels comforting.

passage:
Kindergarten teacher's note, Thursday
During snakes and ladders, Chinmay blew on the dice three times and whispered "six, six, six" before every throw. When he got a six, he shouted, "See! My blowing works!" When he got a one, he said Arnab had "looked at it wrong." Arnab tried blowing too and got a two. Chinmay said Arnab "didn't blow properly." I let them mark their throws on a chart for the rest of the week. We will look at it together on Friday.

qa.q: What did Chinmay whisper before every throw?
qa.a: Six, six, six.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay blow on the dice?
qa.a: He felt excited and in charge, believing his blowing could make a six come up.

qa.q: Why is the throw chart a good idea?
qa.a: Marking all the throws together lets the children see, playfully, that blowing doesn't change the numbers.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel when told he didn't blow properly?
qa.a: Arnab might feel confused or left out, since he tried the same thing.

grounding: A kindergarten teacher records a young boy who believes blowing on the dice makes a six come.

passage: On the day of the village cricket final, little Sahil sat on the wall beside his sister Sarika, wearing his red cap backwards. "If I keep my fingers crossed the whole time, Chacha's team wins," he announced. He crossed them so tight his knuckles went white. When Chacha hit a four, Sahil shouted, "My fingers did that!" When Chacha got out, Sahil looked at his hands. "I let go for one second to scratch my nose." Sarika hid a smile. "Maybe the bowler was just good."

qa.q: What was Sahil wearing?
qa.a: His red cap, backwards.

qa.q: Why did Sahil keep his fingers crossed so tight?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and in charge, believing his crossed fingers could make Chacha's team win.

qa.q: How could Sarika help Sahil without spoiling his fun?
qa.a: Let him enjoy crossing his fingers, while gently showing that the bowler and batters decide the match, as she began to.

qa.q: What might Sarika feel watching Sahil?
qa.a: Sarika seems amused and fond, hiding a smile at his reasoning.

grounding: A young boy believes keeping his fingers crossed decides a cricket match.

passage: Every Saturday Anders watched his father's football team on TV from the same green cushion, holding his left sock in his hand. "If I hold the sock, they score," he told his friend Abebe. That week the team scored twice. "See?" Anders said, waving the sock. The next Saturday Abebe sat on the green cushion first. The team lost. "You sat on my cushion!" Anders cried. Abebe looked at the cushion, then at the TV. "But I wasn't even playing."

qa.q: What did Anders hold while watching?
qa.a: His left sock.

qa.q: Why did Anders blame Abebe for the loss?
qa.a: He felt upset and believed his cushion and sock made the team score, so losing the cushion seemed to cause the loss.

qa.q: What could Anders's father say to help?
qa.a: Gently explain that the players decide the score, and that watching together is the fun part, wherever they sit.

qa.q: How does Abebe see the cushion?
qa.a: Abebe is puzzled, thinking the players, not the cushion, decide the match.

grounding: A young boy believes his cushion and a sock ritual decide his team's result.

passage: On the Diwali party day at the playschool, Sudha miss brought out the big snakes-and-ladders mat. Neelam held the huge foam dice in both hands. She squeezed her eyes shut, blew on it three times, and whispered, "Six, six, six." She threw. Two. "I didn't blow enough!" she cried. On the third turn, she rolled a six and shrieked, "See! My blowing works!" Sudha miss smiled. "Shall we try? Everyone roll without blowing." The children rolled. Some got sixes. Neelam looked puzzled. "The dice doesn't know about my blowing?" "The dice doesn't know anything," Sudha miss said.

qa.q: How many times did Neelam blow on the dice the first time?
qa.a: She blew on it three times.

qa.q: Why did Neelam shriek "See! My blowing works!"?
qa.a: She felt excited and powerful, believing her blowing had made the six happen.

qa.q: How did Sudha miss help Neelam, and how could other adults do the same?
qa.a: She had everyone roll without blowing so Neelam could see sixes still came; adults can gently let children test their rituals.

qa.q: How might the other children feel rolling sixes without blowing?
qa.a: They might feel pleased and surprised, and it shows Neelam that the dice isn't listening to anyone.

grounding: Shows a young child at a Diwali party believing that blowing on the dice can make it roll a six.

passage:
Lohri, first day. Kites filled the sky over Amritsar. Baljeet stood beside his cousin Asif, fingers crossed so hard they hurt. Asif's kite won. "It was my fingers!" Baljeet shouted.
Second day. Baljeet crossed his fingers tighter and hopped on one leg. Asif's kite got cut. Baljeet cried. "I didn't hop enough."
Third day. Asif gave him the spool. "No fingers, no hopping. Just watch." The wind pulled the kite left, then right. It won one fight and lost one. "The wind decides a lot," Asif said. "So I'm not in charge?" "Not of the wind."

qa.q: What did Baljeet say when Asif's kite won on the first day?
qa.a: "It was my fingers!"

qa.q: Why did Baljeet cry on the second day?
qa.a: He felt sad and guilty, believing the kite was cut because he hadn't hopped enough.

qa.q: What did Asif do that helped Baljeet?
qa.a: He let Baljeet hold the spool and watch without rituals, so he could see the wind deciding wins and losses.

qa.q: How might Asif feel when Baljeet blames himself?
qa.a: Asif probably felt fond and a little worried, wanting Baljeet to stop thinking the kite depended on him.

grounding: Shows a young child during Lohri believing crossed fingers and hopping can make a cousin's kite win.

passage: The monsoon rain had knocked out the power, and the Ludo game went on by torchlight. Chaitanya needed a six. He pressed the dice to his forehead and whispered, "Please, please." Six! "It helped!" he shouted. Next roll, he pressed again. Three. His lip shook. "I didn't press hard enough." His older cousin Amandeep held up the torch. "Experiment. Ten rolls with your forehead, ten without." They counted sixes by torchlight: two with, two without. Chaitanya stared at the dice. "It's the same." Amandeep grinned. "The dice can't feel your forehead."

qa.q: How many sixes did Chaitanya get with the forehead and without?
qa.a: Two with, two without.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he rolled a three?
qa.a: He felt upset and guilty, lip shaking, believing he hadn't pressed the dice hard enough.

qa.q: How did Amandeep help Chaitanya test his belief?
qa.a: He suggested ten rolls with and ten without the forehead press, so Chaitanya could see the ritual didn't change the dice.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Chaitanya's forehead ritual?
qa.a: Amandeep sees it as sweet but pointless, and turns it into a fun experiment instead of simply telling Chaitanya off.

grounding: Shows a young child during a monsoon power cut believing that pressing the dice to his forehead makes it roll a six.

passage:
It was Diwali week, and the whole flat smelled of ghee sweets. Deepika and her brother Yash sat on the floor with the ludo board.
"I need a six," Deepika said. She cupped the dice, blew on it three times and squeezed her eyes shut. "Six, six, six."
It rolled a two.
"I didn't blow hard enough," she decided, and on her next turn she blew five times.
Six!
"See?" Deepika bounced on her knees. "I made it!"
Yash opened his mouth, then just smiled and moved his green token.

qa.q: How many times did Deepika blow on the dice the first time?
qa.a: Deepika blew on the dice three times.

qa.q: Why did Deepika feel so happy when the six came?
qa.a: Deepika felt proud and in charge, believing her five hard blows made the dice give a six.

qa.q: How could Yash gently help Deepika another day?
qa.a: Yash could play a round where nobody blows on the dice and count the sixes together, so Deepika sees sixes still come.

qa.q: How does Yash see Deepika's dice ritual?
qa.a: Yash seems to find it sweet and chooses not to argue, letting Deepika enjoy feeling in charge.

grounding: Shows a young child who believes blowing on the dice and wishing hard makes a six come.

passage:
It was a freezing New Year's Eve in Darjeeling, and the heater hummed in front of the TV.
"Don't move!" Chaitanya whispered. "If I keep socks on my hands, our team scores."
"Why socks?" Tenzin asked, pulling his blanket tighter.
"Because last time I did it, they scored."
On the TV, the red team missed.
"You moved your foot," Chaitanya said.
"I didn't!"
"You did. Now sit still. Both hands up."
Tenzin sighed and put both hands up. The red team scored.
"YES!" Chaitanya threw the socks in the air. "We did it!"
"We did it," Tenzin said, grinning, not quite sure how.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya keep on his hands?
qa.a: Chaitanya kept socks on his hands.

qa.q: Why was Chaitanya so sure the socks would help?
qa.a: Last time the team scored while Chaitanya did it, so Chaitanya felt hopeful and in control, sure the ritual would work again.

qa.q: What could a grown-up say to Chaitanya after the match?
qa.a: A grown-up could share the fun and then wonder aloud whether the team might score without socks too, maybe trying it at the next match.

qa.q: How does Tenzin feel about the ritual?
qa.a: Tenzin plays along, a bit puzzled but happy to share the excitement when the team scores.

grounding: Shows a young child who believes a sock ritual and sitting still can make a team score.

passage:
UKG note, sports day in Pongal week. Written by Kiran, class teacher.
During the relay, Lakshmi stood at the side hopping on one foot and whispering, "Blue, blue, blue." When I asked why, she said, "If I hop, Blue House wins."
Blue came second. Lakshmi looked shocked, then said her foot touched the ground by mistake.
In the next race she hopped until her face was red, and Blue won. She ran to me: "I did it!"
What I did next: I hopped with her for a minute, then asked what the runners were doing. "Running very fast," she said. Tomorrow we'll try a dice game with hopping and without.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi whisper while hopping?
qa.a: Lakshmi whispered, 'Blue, blue, blue.'

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi keep hopping until her face was red?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt excited and in charge, believing her hopping could make Blue House win.

qa.q: Why is the dice game with hopping and without a good next step?
qa.a: It lets Lakshmi see for herself whether results change with or without hopping, without anyone laughing at her belief.

qa.q: How might the relay runners see the race?
qa.a: The runners were busy running very fast, and their speed, not the hopping, decided the race.

grounding: Shows a young child who believes her hopping ritual can decide a relay result.

passage: On Diwali afternoon in Nani's village, Yogesh and Harsha played ludo on the courtyard floor. Before every roll, Yogesh blew on the dice, tapped it on his forehead three times and whispered, "Six, six, six." He got a two. "I didn't tap hard enough," he said, and tapped five times. He got a six! "See? It works!" He hugged the dice to his chest. Harsha rolled without any tapping and got a six too. Yogesh frowned. "That was just lucky."

qa.q: What did Yogesh whisper before every roll?
qa.a: "Six, six, six."

qa.q: Why does Yogesh keep tapping the dice on his forehead?
qa.a: Tapping and blowing make him feel in charge of the dice, and that feeling is comforting and exciting, so he believes it really works 🙂

qa.q: How could an adult gently help Yogesh notice what happened?
qa.a: They could count together how many sixes came with tapping and without, like Harsha's six, and laugh about how the dice decides on its own.

qa.q: How might Harsha see the tapping?
qa.a: Harsha may find it funny or puzzling, since Harsha got a six without any tapping at all.

grounding: Shows a young child believing that blowing on and tapping a dice can change what it rolls.
